chapters.title: Chapter 4: Finite Difference Methods for Option Pricing

lessons.title: The Explicit Finite Difference Method: Simplicity and Its Stability Trap

children.text: Lesson 2 left the grid's interior, everything except the three known edges, unresolved. The explicit method is the simplest way to fill it in, a direct, no-system-of-equations formula at every point, built from the same PDE Lesson 1 wrote down. It is also, as this lesson shows with real numbers, the method most likely to fail silently before it fails obviously.

Approximate every derivative in the Black-Scholes PDE at grid point (i, j plus 1), the already-known layer closer to expiry, using neighbouring values on that same layer for the price derivatives, and the gap between layer j and layer j plus 1 for the time derivative.

body.latex: \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \approx \frac{f_{i,j+1}-f_{i,j}}{\Delta t}, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \approx \frac{f_{i+1,j+1}-f_{i-1,j+1}}{2\Delta S}, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2} \approx \frac{f_{i+1,j+1}-2f_{i,j+1}+f_{i-1,j+1}}{\Delta S^2}
body.caption: All three approximations use only the already-known layer j + 1, which is exactly what makes this method explicit, solvable one point at a time, no system of equations required.

children.text: Substitute these into the PDE and solve for the one unknown, f at (i, j), and it collapses to a weighted combination of three known values from layer j plus 1.

body.caption: The explicit update rule. Each unknown point is a direct, three-term combination of known points, one layer closer to expiry.

body.latex: a_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta t\left(\sigma^2 i^2 - r i\right), \quad b_i = 1 - \Delta t\left(\sigma^2 i^2 + r\right), \quad c_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta t\left(\sigma^2 i^2 + r i\right)
body.caption: The three coefficients, using S_i = i times delta-S. This is the standard textbook explicit finite difference formula. Notice the family resemblance to Chapter 2's risk-neutral probability p, three fixed weights combining known neighbours into an unknown value.

children.text: Lesson 2's N = 40 grid turns out to be too coarse in price for real accuracy, regardless of how many time steps are used, a reminder that a finite difference grid has two resolutions to get right, not one. This lesson refines it to N = 200 price steps, delta-S = ₹480, on the same Nifty call, Smax = ₹96,000, sigma = 14%, T = 0.25, r = 6.5%.

body.label: Explicit method, N = 200, M = 20 time steps
body.context: Against the true Black-Scholes price of ₹875.93, about 0.33% off, a genuinely good result

children.text: The standard, textbook safe condition for this method requires every one of a_i, b_i, and c_i to stay non-negative, tightest at the largest i, closest to Smax. For this exact grid, that condition works out to needing at least 195 time steps.

body.text: The ₹873.07 result above used only 20 time steps, well below that 195 threshold. The formal safety condition was already violated when that reasonable-looking answer came out. It did not fail this time. That is exactly the trap, a coefficient going negative does not guarantee immediate visible breakdown, it just removes the guarantee that breakdown won't happen, and it can look completely fine for a while before it doesn't.

body.caption: The same grid, N = 200, as M shrinks further

body.text: Between M = 14 and M = 10, delta-t barely doubles, from about 0.018 to 0.025 years, and the computed price collapses from a perfectly reasonable ₹874.40 to a nonsensical ₹123.22, by way of an equally nonsensical ₹1,049.52 at M = 11. This is not gradual accuracy loss the way Chapter 3's tree oscillation was. It is a cliff.

children.text: A negative coefficient means the update formula is no longer a weighted average of neighbouring values the way Chapter 2's risk-neutral p always was, kept between 0 and 1 by the no-arbitrage condition built back in Lesson 1 of that chapter. Once a coefficient turns negative, small errors at one grid point can get amplified rather than smoothed as they propagate to the next layer, and amplification compounding across many time steps is exactly what produces the runaway, oscillating nonsense seen at M = 11 and M = 10. Chapter 4's remaining lessons introduce methods built specifically to avoid this trap altogether.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the table above, the price is reasonable at M = 14 and completely broken by M = 10, even though the formal stability condition, at least 195 time steps, was already being violated at every single M tested. What does this tell you about that formal condition?
options: The formal condition is wrong and can be ignored
The formal condition is sufficient for guaranteed stability, but violating it does not guarantee immediate visible failure, only that the guarantee no longer holds
The formal condition only applies to put options, not calls
The formal condition means the method always fails below 195 steps
body.explanation: A sufficient condition guarantees the outcome when it holds, it does not promise the opposite outcome when it fails. Every M tested here, including M = 20's reasonable ₹873.07, technically violated the 195-step safety threshold, and most of them still produced sensible answers, until M = 11 and M = 10 didn't. Relying on 'it worked last time despite violating the rule' is precisely the trap.

body.title: A Dangerous Shortcut
body.scenario: A junior quant, under time pressure, sees the M = 20 result above, ₹873.07, looking close to the known Black-Scholes benchmark, and concludes the explicit method with N = 200 and M = 20 is safe to reuse for pricing other, similarly structured options on the desk's book without further checking.
body.prompt: What is the risk in this conclusion, based on what this lesson just demonstrated?
body.modelAnswer: The M = 20 setup already violated the formal stability condition for this specific option's parameters, it simply had not yet crossed into visible breakdown. A different option on the desk, with a different volatility, rate, or Smax, changes the exact coefficients a_i, b_i, and c_i, and could easily land in the danger zone this lesson found between M = 14 and M = 10, or somewhere else entirely, producing a wildly wrong price that looks superficially plausible before someone checks the boundary values carefully. The safe approach is to verify the formal stability condition for each specific set of parameters, not to assume a step count that happened to work once will keep working.

body.text: The explicit method's coefficients are close cousins of the tree's risk-neutral probability, weights combining known values into an unknown one. Where a tree's p is mathematically forced to stay between 0 and 1 by no-arbitrage, the explicit method's weights have no such guarantee, and once they turn negative, the method can look fine for a while before collapsing into nonsense with very little warning.

points: The explicit method approximates every PDE derivative using the already-known layer closer to expiry, giving a direct, three-term formula for each unknown grid point, no system of equations needed.
Its coefficients, a_i, b_i, and c_i, resemble the tree's risk-neutral probability, but are not automatically kept between 0 and 1 the way p is, this is the method's core weakness.
For the Nifty call's N = 200 grid, the formal safe condition requires at least 195 time steps, yet M = 20, well below that, still produced a reasonable ₹873.07.
Reducing time steps further shows a real cliff, ₹874.40 at M = 14 collapsing to ₹123.22 by M = 10, qualitatively different from a tree's bounded oscillation from Chapter 3.

Violating a sufficient stability condition does not guarantee immediate failure, only that the guarantee against failure is gone, which is exactly why the explicit method needs its safe condition checked deliberately rather than inferred from one working example.
